clue.text: Does it involve going to the glaziers for goods?

definitions.text: Does it involve going to the glaziers for goods?

parts.words: Does it involve going to the glaziers for goods?
parts.note: a glazier sells and fits panes of glass, so the pastime of only gazing at shop displays is reread as a literal trip to buy glass

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a certain errand means a trip to the glass-fitter's.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across two lights, 1 and 4. The whole clue is one teasing description: browsing displays without buying is taken literally as shopping for panes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names browsing in store displays without buying, here reread as buying glass panes from a glazier.

clue.text: "Never mind!" might be the answer for some. (Evidently some problem existed to raise the question.)

definitions.text: "Never mind!" might be the answer for some. (Evidently some problem existed to raise the question.)

parts.words: "Never mind!" might be the answer for some. (Evidently some problem existed to raise the question.)
parts.note: the old philosophers' quip pairs mind with its opposite, physical substance, so the brush-off answers the worried question asked when something seems wrong

explanation.surface: Someone asks a sympathetic question and gets brushed off with a breezy reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs down two lights, 1 and 25. Mind and matter are paired in the old philosophers' joke, so 'Never mind!' answers a question that ends in its partner word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the question asked of someone who looks troubled, which the brush-off reply would answer.

clue.text: A specific requirement came first, if so goaded.

parts.note: a need is something specifically required
led means was in front, came first

explanation.surface: A demand arrived ahead of everything else, perhaps because someone was being prodded.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or prod them, so needled and goaded are synonyms.

clue.text: Intense dislike, when you get to act up with the medium's last half.

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to do is to act
the last three of the six letters of medium

explanation.surface: A séance picture: loathing arises when you perform alongside part of a psychic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DO into OD, since this answer is written downwards. 'when you get to' and 'with' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is hatred or strong disapproval felt towards someone, a synonym for intense dislike.

clue.text: See 1
Agitated by the sort that goes other than down.

indicators.note: to sort letters is to put them into a new order, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: the direction that is the opposite of down is up

explanation.surface: Someone is upset by a particular kind of thing that rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sort' reads as 'that kind', but 'sort' acts on 'the', giving HET.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is an informal idiom for excited, worked up or angry, which matches agitated.

clue.text: Peacock-like, in the vernacular. (Such behavior may result in the fall.)

definitions.text: Peacock-like, in the vernacular. (Such behavior may result in the fall.)

parts.words: Peacock-like, in the vernacular. (Such behavior may result in the fall.)
parts.note: the everyday simile is 'as ... as a peacock', and the proverb says pride goes before a fall

explanation.walkthrough: Two familiar sayings point to one word: the common simile about peacocks, and the proverb that conceit comes before a downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: A peacock fanning its tail is the stock image of vanity and self-satisfaction, and the proverb warns that such arrogance leads to ruin.

clue.text: Incised carvings not found out with the price printed–51, according to the Romans.

parts.note: someone not out is in, at home
a tag is the label with the printed price
LI is 51 in Roman numerals: L is 50 and I is 1

explanation.surface: A shopper hunts for engraved gems, checks the price label and finds the Roman figure on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Italian plural of intaglio, a gem or seal with a design cut into its surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Intaglio work cuts the design below the surface, so these are engravings sunk into the material rather than raised.

clue.text: A political party with the lady said to go on errands, one hears.

definitions.text: said to go on errands, one hears

parts.note: GOP, the Grand Old Party, is the US Republican Party
her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: A party and a woman are sent out to run errands.
explanation.walkthrough: The built word is the burrowing rodent, but spoken it is identical to gofer, someone who goes for things: 'said' and 'one hears' make the definition a matter of sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A gofer is an assistant who runs errands, and the animal's name is pronounced the same way.

clue.text: Composer–a person with no belief in one finally.

parts.note: a pagan is one outside the established faith, an unbeliever
one is the numeral I, which comes at the end

explanation.surface: A composer is described as a nonbeliever who finally comes round to one faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' tells you the Roman-numeral one goes last. Calling a pagan a person with no belief is loose: strictly a pagan lacks the main faith, not all faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolò Paganini was an Italian violinist who also wrote music, including the famous caprices for solo violin.

clue.text: The sort of camera I see represented in the Nation?

indicators.note: presented again in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A photographer wonders what kind of camera appears in the magazine's pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' rearranges CAMERA and I. The Nation is the US weekly in which this puzzle appeared, so 'the Nation' doubles as the country it serves.
explanation.definitionFit: The United States is the country, the nation, for the magazine's readers, and the magazine's title plays on that.

clue.text: A couple with backward favorites might start the dance off.

parts.note: a couple is two

indicators.note: backward means the word for favorites is written back to front

parts.note: pets are favourites, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A pair with their beloved companions opens the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-step is a ballroom dance, the kind that could open an evening's dancing.

clue.text: A witching place for misbehaving males.

indicators.note: letters that misbehave are out of their proper order, so the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A town where badly behaved men were accused of sorcery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misbehaving' rearranges MALES. SALEM is the Massachusetts town of the 1692 witch trials.
explanation.definitionFit: Salem is famous for its witch trials, so it is the classic place associated with witchcraft.

clue.text: Possibly a bad striker found in 28.

indicators.note: the letters are found in that answer, rearranged into a new word

parts.note: the answer at 28 across is the word for a resort with healing waters

explanation.surface: A poor hitter turns up in a numbered spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 28 across, SPA; 'found in' says the snake's letters are found there, reordered. 'Possibly' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A venomous snake strikes at its prey, so an asp is one example of a dangerous striker.

clue.text: Perhaps Fido, that is–or a little one that was told to get along in song.

definitions.text: a little one that was told to get along in song

parts.note: Fido is a classic dog's name, so this is an example
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A pet called Fido is compared with a young animal from a cowboy ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: A dogie is a motherless calf; the cowboy song goes 'Git along, little dogies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The calves in the Western song are urged to keep moving along the trail by the singing cowhands.

clue.text: A helluva place, but you can always find it in the shade.

indicators.text: you can always find it in
indicators.note: the letters can always be found inside the next word, by rearranging them

explanation.surface: A joke about a hot place you can still find in the cool of the shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Hades is the underworld of Greek myth, used as a polite word for hell, which fits a helluva place.

clue.text: Deep, poetically.

parts.note: in poetry 'the deep' stands for the ocean

explanation.walkthrough: A noun use of 'deep' found in verse and hymns, as in 'those in peril on the deep'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poets call the ocean 'the deep', so the word is a literary name for the open water.

clue.text: The little devil has legal approval, which is understood.

parts.note: an imp is a small devil
licit means lawful, approved by law

explanation.surface: A mischievous child is granted lawful permission.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implicit is implied rather than stated, so it is tacitly understood.

clue.text: How the girl's hair was arranged certainly would have ended in a curl like Porky had.

definitions.text: How the girl's hair was arranged
definitions.meaning: first meaning: plaits hanging at the back or sides of the head

definitions.text: would have ended in a curl like Porky had
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the curly tails of pigs, like that of the cartoon character Porky Pig

explanation.walkthrough: 'certainly' is a link word. Porky Pig is the stuttering Warner Bros. cartoon pig.
explanation.definitionFit: The braided hairstyle takes its name from the curly appendage of a pig, which is what the second half describes literally.

clue.text: Perhaps aid the old comedian's wife.

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way, so the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A vaudeville comic's wife may be a helper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges AID. Ida was the wife of the comedian Eddie Cantor, who sang and joked about her.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddie Cantor, the old-time radio comedian, often mentioned his wife by name, so she is the famous comedian's spouse.

clue.text: An uninvited guest in the junction, more impolite.

parts.note: a T-junction, where one road meets another, gives the letter
ruder means more impolite

explanation.surface: A gatecrasher at the crossroads behaves even worse.
explanation.definitionFit: An intruder enters where they are not wanted, so they are a guest nobody asked to come.

clue.text: The hard up might be doing it, which one hears is enjoying the pool by oneself.

definitions.text: The hard up might be doing it

indicators.note: the phrase as heard is the same as the answer

parts.note: lying on the water's surface with nobody else in the pool, said as a phrase

explanation.surface: Poor people might be up to something that sounds like a solitary swim.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across two lights, 21 and 23. 'one hears' says the answer sounds like drifting solo in the pool, FLOATING ALONE; 'which' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone short of money may raise funds by arranging to borrow, the idiom being to float a loan.

clue.text: To feel bad getting up is no return for more than a brief encounter.

indicators.note: in a down entry, getting up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to ail is to be unwell

indicators.note: a return goes back the other way, so the word is written backwards

explanation.surface: Feeling ill on rising is no recompense for a lasting affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting up' turns AIL into LIA; 'return' turns NO into ON. 'for' is a link word. Brief Encounter is the 1945 film about a short romance.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a love affair, something longer than the fleeting meeting of the film title.

clue.text: See 21
The more stars or bars you display, the better chance that you do, as far as the next fellow is concerned.

definitions.text: The more stars or bars you display, the better chance that you do, as far as the next fellow is concerned.

parts.words: The more stars or bars you display, the better chance that you do, as far as the next fellow is concerned.
parts.note: military insignia of stars and bars show seniority, so more of them means being senior to the officer beside you

explanation.walkthrough: Stars and bars are badges of rank on uniforms; whoever wears more stands above the other man.
explanation.definitionFit: To outrank someone is to hold a higher grade, which officers show through the insignia on their uniforms.

clue.text: See 1
In the capital, a most memorable spot.

indicators.note: the answer is contained in the letters of the next words, running across the word break

parts.note: the letters run from the end of capital through a into the start of most

explanation.surface: A sightseer singles out the most unforgettable place in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' says the answer sits inside 'capital, a most'. 'Remember the Alamo!' was the Texan battle cry after the 1836 siege, which is why the spot is memorable.
explanation.definitionFit: The Texan rallying cry told everyone to keep the mission fortress in mind, making it a place to remember.

clue.text: Rosie is upset by a willow branch arrangement.

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman named Rosie is annoyed by a display of cut willow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is upset' rearranges ROSIE. The definition sits in the middle; 'a', 'by' and 'arrangement' are link words, the last repeating the idea of rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a kind of willow whose pliable shoots are used in basketwork.

clue.text: Pa's out of place here, but he might go there for a good scrubbing.

definitions.text: he might go there for a good scrubbing

indicators.note: letters out of place are moved to a new order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Father feels awkward here but would visit for a thorough wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' rearranges PAS; 'here, but' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a resort with mineral baths, where people go to bathe and be cleaned up.

clue.text: One might be obedient on another's.

definitions.text: One might be obedient on another's.

parts.words: One might be obedient on another's.
parts.note: the clue is a sentence with its last word left out: one obeys on another person's authority

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word completes the phrase 'on someone's ...', meaning on their authority or word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's say-so is their command or permission, the thing an obedient person acts on.

clue.text: Where Walter was told to take the lead, in song.

definitions.text: Where Walter was told to take the lead, in song.

parts.words: Where Walter was told to take the lead, in song.
parts.note: the popular song 'Walter, Walter, lead me to the' place where weddings happen

explanation.walkthrough: The 1930s song, sung by Gracie Fields, has a woman begging Walter to lead her to the wedding spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer wants to be married, so she asks to be led to the church table where vows are said.

clue.text: Representive of a bloke, as the Brit says.

parts.note: gent, short for gentleman, is a British word for a man, a bloke

explanation.surface: Something typical of an ordinary man, in British speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, 'a gent'. 'of' is a link word, and 'Representive' is the clue's spelling of representative.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent acts on behalf of someone else, so an agent is a representative.

clue.text: An examination, if your head is necessary to finish it, as you might swear!

parts.note: a test is an examination

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: An exasperated student whose exam needs some brainwork to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'head' of 'your' is Y, and 'is necessary to finish it' places it last; 'as you might' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To testify is to state something under oath, as a witness swears in court.

clue.text: Caribbean islands–picture the slippery type, if backward.

indicators.note: backward means the combined letters are read back to front

parts.note: to draw is to picture
an eel is proverbially slippery

explanation.surface: A tourist tries to sketch slippery fish around the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: DRAW then EEL gives DRAWEEL, and 'if backward' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leeward Islands are the northern group of the Lesser Antilles in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Manages the social upheaval–and really throws things around!

parts.note: to run something is to manage it
a riot is a violent public disturbance

explanation.surface: An organiser of a disturbance who is truly hurling objects.
explanation.definitionFit: To run riot is to behave in a wild, uncontrolled way, tossing things about.

clue.text: Such as Bram should be able to tend the fire.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Bram ..., the author of Dracula, so a person with this surname

definitions.text: should be able to tend the fire
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a person who feeds fuel to a furnace

explanation.walkthrough: The author of Dracula carried an occupational surname, and the clue suggests he should be good at that job.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoker shovels coal into a furnace or boiler, and the Irish novelist's name is the same word.
